action.title: ACME Engineering Handbook
action.body:
# ACME Engineering Handbook

This is the working handbook for ACME Engineering. ACME builds a multi-tenant commerce platform used by retailers to accept orders, coordinate fulfillment, and integrate their internal systems through APIs and webhooks.

Humans and software agents work from the same durable engineering knowledge. Agents are useful because they can discover context, execute repeatable procedures, and prepare changes quickly; humans remain accountable for product, operational, and security decisions.

## Start here

- [[Engineering organization]] — teams, ownership, and escalation paths.
- Platform architecture — how the production system fits together.
- Service catalog — owned production systems and their operational tier.
- Decision register — durable architecture and product-interface decisions.
- Q3 2026 engineering priorities — what the organization is changing now.
- Shared engineering skills — reusable procedures for humans and agents.
- Incident review index — incidents, postmortems, and follow-through.
- Human-agent engineering model — how we delegate work without creating a second knowledge system.
- On-call handbook — how we operate production.
- [[Engineering glossary]] — shared language and system names.

## How we use this space

Keep durable knowledge here: architecture, decisions, runbooks, incident learning, project context, and reusable skills. Chat, tickets, terminals, and agent sessions can carry the immediate conversation; this handbook should preserve what a future engineer or agent needs to understand after that conversation disappears.

A skill is not a substitute for the source material it references. The skill describes a reliable way to perform a class of work and links back to the services, policies, decisions, and runbooks that constrain it.

If a document changes materially, update it rather than creating a near-duplicate. If an incident or review exposes a better procedure, improve the relevant skill as part of closing the loop.

action.title: Engineering organization
action.body:
# Engineering organization

ACME Engineering has four operating groups. Teams own outcomes and production systems; ownership includes documentation, observability, on-call health, and lifecycle decisions.

## Product Engineering

Builds merchant-facing workflows and the web application. See [[Team: Product Engineering]] and Merchant Console.

## Core Services

Owns APIs and transaction services that sit on the critical order path. See [[Team: Core Services]] and Checkout API.

## Platform & Reliability

Owns shared runtime infrastructure, delivery systems, databases, observability, and incident practice. See [[Team: Platform & Reliability]].

## Security

Sets security architecture, reviews high-risk changes, and owns identity controls. See Team: Security Engineering.

Engineering managers own staffing and delivery. Technical ownership remains explicit at the service and project level; an escalation should never depend on knowing which person happens to remember a subsystem.

## Humans and agents

Teams may delegate research, code preparation, documentation work, and operational analysis to authorized agents. Delegation does not transfer ownership: the owning team still decides what is correct, what may ship, and what may mutate production. Shared procedures live in Shared engineering skills, and organization-wide boundaries live in Agent access and approval policy.

action.title: Q3 2026 engineering priorities
action.body:
# Q3 2026 engineering priorities

The quarter is intentionally narrow. Reliability work takes precedence over expanding surface area in the public API.

## 1. Finish Project Relay

Move webhook fan-out off the synchronous checkout path. The accepted design is in [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]]. Track execution in [[Project Relay]].

## 2. Reduce checkout tail latency

Bring Checkout API p99 below 700 ms during peak traffic and eliminate connection-pool exhaustion as an incident class. See Checkout API and INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike.

## 3. Complete API v2 migration

Reach 90% of active integrations on v2 before announcing a v1 sunset date. See [[API v2 migration]].

## 4. Tighten operational readiness

Every tier-1 service must have an owner, SLO, dashboard, rollback path, and tested runbook. The baseline is Service ownership standard.

### Explicitly not a priority

A broad service decomposition. We will split systems only when ownership, scaling, or failure isolation requires it; smaller services are not a goal by themselves.

action.title: Team: Product Engineering
action.body:
# Product Engineering

**Manager:** Grace  
**Mission:** Make complex commerce operations understandable and fast for merchant teams.

## Owned areas

- [[Merchant Console]]
- Order-management workflows
- Integration setup and diagnostics
- Frontend platform conventions

## Current work

The team is supporting API v2 migration with in-product migration tooling while keeping the console within the [[Web performance budget]].

## Working agreements

Product engineers can merge routine changes after review and green CI. Changes that alter authentication, public API behavior, data retention, or tier-1 failure modes require review from the owning specialist team.

The team rotates a weekday support engineer who triages merchant-facing regressions before they reach the platform on-call.

action.title: Team: Core Services
action.body:
# Core Services

**Tech lead:** Bob  
**Mission:** Keep ACME's transactional APIs predictable under load and safe to evolve.

## Owned services

- Checkout API
- Order Service
- Public API compatibility layer

Core Services is the primary engineering owner for API v2 migration and a partner on Project Relay.

## Design posture

Prefer explicit transactional boundaries, boring storage, and observable failure modes. We do not introduce a queue, cache, or new service merely to reduce local code complexity. Architecture changes should state the operational cost they add as clearly as the feature they enable.

Tier-1 production changes follow Production release process and must have a rollback or forward-fix plan before deployment begins.

## Agent-assisted work

Core Services commonly uses agents to trace call paths, compare API schemas, prepare mechanical migrations, and draft implementation plans. Public behavior is reviewed against Public API compatibility policy using Skill: Review a public API change. Agents preparing code follow Skill: Implement a repository change and must surface uncertainty rather than silently choosing compatibility behavior.

action.title: Team: Platform & Reliability
action.body:
# Platform & Reliability

**Lead:** Charlie  
**Mission:** Give product teams a production platform that is understandable, recoverable, and difficult to misuse.

## Owned areas

- PostgreSQL, Redis, and runtime infrastructure
- Build and deployment systems
- Metrics, logs, tracing, and alerting
- On-call handbook and incident practice
- Shared event-delivery infrastructure used by Webhook Gateway

## Current focus

Project Relay is the largest platform change this quarter. The team is also applying the database lessons from Postmortem: INC-2026-017 and testing Runbook: Database failover during the next game day.

Platform does not own application correctness for other teams. It owns the paved road and joins incidents when shared infrastructure is plausibly involved.

## Agent-assisted operations

Platform agents can gather read-only production context, correlate telemetry, prepare release packets, and walk engineers through established runbooks. They never become incident commander and do not perform production mutations merely because a runbook contains the command. Start with Skill: Triage a production incident and Agent access and approval policy.

action.title: Team: Security Engineering
action.body:
# Security Engineering

**Lead:** Eve  
**Mission:** Reduce security risk without turning security review into a separate delivery system.

## Owned areas

- Authentication and authorization architecture
- Secrets and key-management standards
- Threat modeling for high-risk changes
- Incident support for suspected security events

Start with [[Authentication model]] and [[Data classification and handling]].

## Review triggers

Security review is required for new credential types, cross-tenant data access, externally reachable administration paths, encryption-key changes, and new classes of retained sensitive data.

Routine implementation inside an already-reviewed design stays with the owning product team. Security Engineering should define reusable constraints rather than repeatedly approve the same class of change.

Security also owns the organization-wide constraints for agent credentials and privileged actions. See [[Agent access and approval policy]]. Agent-generated security analysis is treated as input to review, not as approval.

action.title: Platform architecture
action.body:
# Platform architecture

ACME serves merchant users through [[Merchant Console]] and machine integrations through [[Checkout API]]. Both ultimately operate on order state owned by [[Order Service]].

## Request path

1. Edge routing terminates TLS and applies coarse request limits.
2. Checkout API authenticates the merchant or integration and validates the request.
3. Order Service performs the authoritative order transition in PostgreSQL.
4. Domain events are committed with the transaction and later delivered by [[Webhook Gateway]].

## Data

PostgreSQL is the system of record for transactional state. Redis is disposable acceleration and coordination state; no business fact may exist only in Redis. Object storage holds exports and large merchant-generated artifacts.

## Reliability boundaries

Checkout may complete while downstream webhook delivery is delayed. That boundary is deliberate and documented in ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction.

For the active redesign of webhook delivery, see Project Relay and RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery.

action.title: Checkout API
action.body:
# Checkout API

**Tier:** 1  
**Owner:** Core Services  
**Primary datastore:** PostgreSQL through Order Service

Checkout API is the public synchronous entry point for creating and updating checkout sessions. It validates integration credentials, normalizes requests, applies idempotency rules, and coordinates the order transition with [[Order Service]].

## Reliability target

- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly
- p95 latency target: < 300 ms
- p99 latency target: < 700 ms

Webhook delivery is not part of the synchronous success condition. See ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction.

## Common failure modes

The most important historical failure was database connection starvation during a traffic spike. See INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike and Postmortem: INC-2026-017. Operational response starts with Runbook: Checkout latency.

API compatibility expectations are documented in Public API compatibility policy.

action.title: Order Service
action.body:
# Order Service

**Tier:** 1  
**Owner:** Core Services

Order Service owns the authoritative state machine for carts, orders, payment intent references, and fulfillment status. Other services may cache or project order state but may not mutate order records directly.

## Storage rules

All externally visible state transitions are committed in PostgreSQL. Events that describe those transitions are written transactionally and consumed asynchronously. This keeps the business state recoverable even when downstream systems are unavailable.

## Interfaces

- synchronous internal API used by [[Checkout API]];
- transactional outbox consumed by [[Webhook Gateway]];
- read projections used by [[Merchant Console]].

Schema changes must remain compatible with the currently deployed application version during rolling deployments. High-risk migrations require a staged expand/migrate/contract plan and a tested rollback boundary.

action.title: Webhook Gateway
action.body:
# Webhook Gateway

**Tier:** 1  
**Owners:** Platform & Reliability + Core Services

Webhook Gateway delivers merchant event notifications to external HTTPS endpoints. Delivery is at-least-once; consumers must deduplicate by event ID.

## Current architecture

The gateway reads committed order events, schedules delivery attempts, records attempt state, and applies bounded exponential backoff. A merchant endpoint cannot block checkout completion.

## Limits

- 10 second per-attempt timeout
- 24 hour retry window
- per-tenant concurrency cap
- payloads are immutable after event publication

The current queue-backed design was approved in [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]] and is being rolled out through Project Relay. The original separation from checkout is recorded in ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction.

Operational guidance: Runbook: Webhook backlog.

action.title: Merchant Console
action.body:
# Merchant Console

**Owner:** Product Engineering

Merchant Console is the React application used by operations teams to inspect orders, manage integrations, configure webhooks, and investigate delivery failures.

## Architectural constraints

The console consumes public or public-shaped APIs wherever practical so internal UI paths do not silently acquire capabilities unavailable to integrations. Privileged administrative actions use separate endpoints and explicit authorization checks.

## Current work

The v2 integration setup flow is part of API v2 migration. Performance regressions are evaluated against Web performance budget.

## Supportability

Error states should expose a stable request or event identifier that support engineers can use to correlate browser reports with backend traces. Avoid generic “something went wrong” states for known server errors.

action.title: ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction
action.body:
# ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction

## Status

Accepted.

## Context

Early checkout code attempted the first merchant webhook delivery before returning success. A slow or failing merchant endpoint therefore increased checkout latency and coupled ACME availability to infrastructure outside our control.

## Decision

Checkout success means the order transition and its event are durably committed. Webhook delivery happens asynchronously after commit and is never required for the checkout request to succeed.

## Consequences

- Merchants observe eventual rather than immediate notification.
- Delivery must be at-least-once and externally deduplicatable.
- We need durable retry state and backlog visibility.
- Support tooling must distinguish “order committed” from “webhook delivered.”

The implementation is owned by Webhook Gateway. The next iteration of the delivery system is specified in [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]].

action.title: RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery
action.body:
# RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery

## Status

Proposed.

## Problem

The current webhook workers use a database polling loop that is reliable but increasingly expensive at peak volume. Large tenants can also create enough retries to delay unrelated tenants.

## Proposal

Introduce a durable queue between the transactional outbox and delivery workers. Partition scheduling by tenant, enforce per-tenant concurrency, and keep delivery-attempt history in PostgreSQL for support and auditability.

## Invariants

- Order Service remains the source of event truth.
- A queue message is a delivery instruction, not the only copy of an event.
- Duplicate delivery remains valid behavior.
- Rebuilding queue state from PostgreSQL must be possible.

## Rollout

Shadow-enqueue first, then enable delivery for internal tenants, then 5%, 25%, and 100% of production tenants. Rollback returns scheduling to the database poller without changing event IDs.

Implementation is tracked in [[Project Relay]].

action.title: Public API compatibility policy
action.body:
# Public API compatibility policy

ACME treats documented public API behavior as a product contract.

## Compatible changes

Adding optional response fields, adding new endpoints, and accepting additional enum values are normally compatible. Clients must ignore response fields they do not understand.

## Breaking changes

Removing or renaming fields, changing validation meaningfully, narrowing accepted values, or changing authentication semantics requires a new API version or an explicit migration plan.

## Deprecation

A deprecation needs a replacement path, usage telemetry, a named owner, and direct communication to affected high-volume integrations. We do not announce a removal date until the migration path is proven in production.

[[API v2 migration]] follows this policy. Security fixes may require a shorter path, but the exception and rationale must be documented.

action.title: Project Relay
action.body:
# Project Relay

**Owner:** Charlie  
**Status:** In progress  
**Target:** 100% production webhook traffic by 2026-09-18

Relay implements [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]] for Webhook Gateway. The goal is to isolate tenants during retry storms and remove database polling load without weakening delivery durability.

## Milestones

- [x] Queue provisioning and metrics
- [x] Shadow enqueue from production outbox
- [ ] Internal tenants on queue-backed delivery
- [ ] 5% production canary
- [ ] 25% production
- [ ] 100% production
- [ ] Remove old scheduler after two stable weeks

## Guardrails

The old poller remains deployable until the final cleanup milestone. Event IDs and attempt history do not change during rollout. A rollback must not require a data migration.

## Success measures

Webhook scheduling p99 under 2 seconds, no cross-tenant starvation in load tests, and at least 40% lower polling queries on the primary database.

action.title: API v2 migration
action.body:
# API v2 migration

**Owner:** Dave  
**Status:** Active

API v2 removes several ambiguous v1 field names, makes idempotency behavior consistent across write endpoints, and standardizes error envelopes.

## Current adoption

Approximately 64% of active integration traffic is on v2. The largest remaining blockers are two high-volume merchants with generated clients and several long-tail integrations that have not been touched in more than a year.

## Migration plan

1. Keep v1 and v2 behavior independently observable.
2. Provide request/response examples for every changed endpoint.
3. Surface migration status in Merchant Console.
4. Contact high-volume v1 integrations directly.
5. Reach 90% active traffic before proposing a sunset date.

The migration is governed by [[Public API compatibility policy]]. No v1 removal date has been approved.

action.title: On-call handbook
action.body:
# On-call handbook

The on-call engineer protects customer impact first and optimizes explanation second. Escalate early when the failure crosses an ownership boundary or the blast radius is unclear.

## During an incident

1. Establish whether customers are affected.
2. Create an incident channel and name an incident lead for SEV-1/SEV-2.
3. Prefer reversible mitigation over speculative root-cause fixes.
4. Keep a short timestamped timeline of meaningful actions.
5. Hand off explicitly if the incident crosses a shift boundary.

## Severity

- **SEV-1:** widespread inability to transact or security compromise.
- **SEV-2:** significant degradation or partial outage with material customer impact.
- **SEV-3:** limited degradation with a safe workaround.

Start from the service-specific runbook: [[Runbook: Checkout latency]], [[Runbook: Webhook backlog]], or [[Runbook: Database failover]].

After meaningful incidents, create a blameless postmortem focused on system conditions and follow-through. See [[Postmortem: INC-2026-017]].

## Using agents during incidents

An authorized agent may collect read-only context, correlate dashboards and recent changes, maintain a draft timeline, and propose the next diagnostic step. The incident commander remains a human. Any production mutation, customer communication, failover, rollback, or security-sensitive action requires the approval defined by Agent access and approval policy.

For a consistent starting point use Skill: Triage a production incident. Service-specific procedures such as Skill: Investigate checkout latency remain subordinate to the runbook and current incident command.

action.title: Runbook: Checkout latency
action.body:
# Runbook: Checkout latency

Use when Checkout API p99 exceeds 1 second for 5 minutes or checkout error rate rises with database wait time.

## Triage

1. Confirm customer impact and open the Checkout overview dashboard.
2. Compare application latency with PostgreSQL connection wait, query latency, and CPU.
3. Check whether one tenant or endpoint dominates traffic.
4. Check deploy history before changing infrastructure.

## Safe mitigations

- Roll back the most recent Checkout deployment if timing correlates.
- Reduce nonessential background work against the primary database.
- Apply the documented per-tenant traffic guard if a single tenant is saturating capacity.

Do **not** raise the application connection-pool limit without checking database headroom; that amplified [[INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike]].

If the primary database is unhealthy rather than saturated, follow [[Runbook: Database failover]].

action.title: Runbook: Webhook backlog
action.body:
# Runbook: Webhook backlog

Use when oldest undelivered webhook age exceeds 10 minutes or scheduled delivery lag is growing continuously.

## Triage

1. Determine whether enqueue, scheduling, or outbound delivery is the bottleneck.
2. Compare backlog by tenant; one retry storm should not consume all workers.
3. Check outbound error classes: timeout, DNS, TLS, 4xx, and 5xx.
4. Verify queue consumers are making forward progress before scaling them.

## Mitigation

Increase worker capacity only when downstream connection and database headroom exist. If one tenant dominates retries, lower that tenant's concurrency before changing global limits.

During Project Relay rollout, disable the queue-backed scheduler for affected cohorts if lag is caused by the new path; the database scheduler remains the rollback mechanism.

Never delete delivery attempts to make the backlog metric look healthy.

action.title: Runbook: Database failover
action.body:
# Runbook: Database failover

This procedure is for loss or severe degradation of the primary transactional PostgreSQL instance. Ordinary query saturation should be handled at the application layer first.

## Preconditions

- Incident lead named.
- Replication health checked.
- Candidate replica is within the accepted recovery-point window.
- Application teams warned that a short write interruption is expected.

## Procedure

1. Stop automated deploys.
2. Fence the unhealthy primary where possible.
3. Promote the selected replica using the database provider control plane.
4. Update the primary endpoint and verify TLS identity.
5. Run read and write smoke tests through Checkout API.
6. Watch error rate, replication, and connection churn for 30 minutes.

Do not fail back during the same incident unless the promoted instance is itself unsafe. Recovery work should be a separate, reviewed change.

action.title: Service ownership standard
Production release process
action.body:
# Production release process

ACME deploys continuously during staffed hours. A release is a normal engineering operation, not a ceremony, but tier-1 changes need a clear recovery path.

## Before deploy

- CI green on the exact revision.
- Database changes are backward compatible with the currently running version.
- Metrics or logs exist for the behavior being changed.
- Operator knows the rollback or forward-fix boundary.

## Rollout

Prefer a small canary when behavior can be meaningfully segmented. Watch service SLOs and the changed behavior, not only host-level health.

## Stop conditions

Pause or roll back on unexplained error-rate increase, material latency regression, or evidence of corrupted state. Do not continue a rollout merely because the error budget technically allows it.

Incidents during release follow On-call handbook. High-risk database changes should reference Runbook: Database failover only as disaster recovery, not as a migration strategy.

## Agent preparation

Agents may prepare the release packet: summarize changes, verify linked decisions, identify migration or rollback steps, and collect CI evidence using Skill: Prepare a production release. A human release owner confirms the packet and initiates production deployment. Preparation authority is not deployment authority.

action.title: INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike
action.body:
# INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike

**Severity:** SEV-2  
**Status:** Resolved  
**Service:** Checkout API

On 2026-08-14 from 16:07–16:31 UTC, checkout p99 latency exceeded 4 seconds and approximately 7.8% of checkout requests returned 5xx responses.

## Timeline

- **16:07** — latency alert fired.
- **16:10** — on-call observed PostgreSQL connection wait increasing rapidly.
- **16:14** — recent application deploy ruled out.
- **16:18** — team reduced concurrency for a high-volume bulk-import tenant.
- **16:22** — connection wait began recovering.
- **16:31** — error rate and p99 returned to baseline.

## Immediate finding

A bulk-import traffic burst exhausted the application's database pool. Increasing pool size during initial mitigation increased contention at PostgreSQL and briefly worsened tail latency.

Full analysis and follow-up are in [[Postmortem: INC-2026-017]].

action.title: Postmortem: INC-2026-017
action.body:
# Postmortem: INC-2026-017

## Summary

A bulk-import traffic burst caused Checkout API workers to saturate their PostgreSQL connection pool. Requests queued behind connection acquisition, then retried close enough together to increase pressure. The first mitigation—raising the application pool limit—shifted contention into PostgreSQL and made tail latency worse for several minutes.

## Why safeguards did not catch it

Load tests modeled aggregate request volume but not one tenant producing a burst of expensive writes. Alerts emphasized query duration and CPU; connection-acquisition wait was visible on dashboards but did not page.

## What worked

Per-tenant traffic controls existed and were applied without deployment. Once concurrency was reduced, the system recovered predictably.

## Actions

- Add connection-acquisition wait to the Checkout SLO dashboard.
- Load-test tenant-skewed traffic before the next peak event.
- Cap bulk-import concurrency independently from interactive checkout.
- Update [[Runbook: Checkout latency]] to warn against unreviewed pool expansion.

No individual action caused the incident; the failure came from capacity assumptions and a mitigation path that was insufficiently documented.

action.title: Authentication model
action.body:
# Authentication model

ACME has separate credential classes for human users and machine integrations. They may share authorization concepts, but they do not share credentials.

## Human access

Merchant Console uses short-lived browser sessions established through the identity service. Administrative roles require phishing-resistant MFA. Session revocation must take effect without waiting for token expiry.

## Machine access

Public API integrations use scoped credentials tied to one merchant tenant. Credentials are shown only at creation, stored hashed where verification permits, and can be individually revoked.

## Authorization invariants

- Tenant identity is derived from authenticated context, never accepted from an untrusted request body.
- Cross-tenant support access is explicit, audited, and time-bounded.
- Service-to-service credentials do not imply merchant authorization.

Changes to credential types or cross-tenant access require Security Engineering review. Data sensitivity expectations are in [[Data classification and handling]].

action.title: Data classification and handling
action.body:
# Data classification and handling

ACME uses three practical data classes.

## Public

Information intentionally published by ACME. No special storage restrictions.

## Internal

Engineering and business information not intended for public distribution: architecture notes, operational metrics, internal identifiers, and most logs.

## Restricted

Credentials, authentication secrets, payment-related tokens, private customer content, and data whose disclosure could enable cross-tenant access or account takeover.

Restricted data must not appear in normal application logs, issue screenshots, or ad-hoc analytics exports. Secrets belong in the managed secret store and must be individually rotatable.

Production access should be the minimum needed for the task and should leave an audit trail. A new class of retained restricted data requires Security Engineering review and a documented retention purpose.

For identity-specific constraints see [[Authentication model]].

## Agent handling

Agents receive the same minimum-necessary access rule as humans, but access must also be appropriate for the runtime in which the agent executes. Do not place secrets or restricted production data into general-purpose prompts, skill text, or durable notes. [[Agent access and approval policy]] defines the approval boundaries for agent actions.

action.title: Web performance budget
action.body:
# Web performance budget

The Merchant Console should remain usable on ordinary business laptops and imperfect office networks. Performance work is evaluated against user-visible interaction, not bundle size alone.

## Budgets

For the authenticated order list on a warm CDN path:

- initial JavaScript transfer: <= 350 KB compressed;
- Largest Contentful Paint p75: < 2.5 s;
- Interaction to Next Paint p75: < 200 ms;
- route transition to useful content p75: < 800 ms.

## Review triggers

A change that adds more than 25 KB compressed JavaScript to the shared shell needs a short justification. Large optional features should load behind the route or interaction that needs them.

The budget is a constraint for Merchant Console, not a reason to avoid functionality. If a requirement genuinely needs more client code, record the tradeoff and update the budget deliberately rather than silently exceeding it.

action.title: New engineer onboarding
action.body:
# New engineer onboarding

The goal of the first week is to build a correct mental model of ACME, not to maximize merged pull requests.

## Day 1–2

- Read [[ACME Engineering Handbook]] and [[Engineering organization]].
- Follow Platform architecture end to end.
- Set up local development and request only the production access required for your role.
- Pair with your team's support or on-call engineer for one real customer issue.

## Day 3–5

- Read one service page owned by your team and its runbook.
- Read INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike and Postmortem: INC-2026-017 to understand how we document failure.
- Ship one small production-safe improvement through Production release process.

By the end of week two, a new engineer should know where their team boundary ends, which systems are tier-1, and how to find the decision behind a non-obvious architectural constraint.

## Working with agents

ACME does not maintain a separate set of "AI docs." Agents and engineers use the same service catalog, architecture, decisions, runbooks, and project pages. Read Human-agent engineering model and browse Shared engineering skills before delegating repository or production work.

When an agent discovers durable context that is missing, the expected end state is not a better private prompt. Capture it back into the relevant Kival object or improve the reusable skill with Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge.

action.title: Engineering glossary
action.body:
# Engineering glossary

**Checkout** — the synchronous API workflow that validates and commits an order transition through Checkout API.

**Event** — an immutable record that a business state transition occurred. Events originate from Order Service.

**Delivery attempt** — one outbound attempt by Webhook Gateway to send an event to a merchant endpoint.

**Tier-1** — a service whose failure can materially prevent merchants from transacting. Tier-1 ownership requirements are in Service ownership standard.

**Tenant** — one merchant's isolated ACME account and data boundary.

**Relay** — the queue-backed webhook delivery project described in Project Relay.

**Canary** — a deliberately small production cohort used to observe a change before wider rollout.

Prefer these terms in durable documentation. If a concept needs a paragraph to disambiguate repeatedly, add it here rather than relying on team-local vocabulary.

action.title: Service catalog
action.body:
# Service catalog

This catalog is the shared service map for engineers and agents. Ownership, tier, dependencies, and operational links should be discoverable here before anyone starts changing or diagnosing a service.

The catalog lists systems with durable production ownership. It is intentionally smaller than the repository list: libraries and short-lived jobs belong here only when they carry an operational boundary of their own.

## Tier 1

- [[Checkout API]] — Core Services — synchronous merchant transaction path.
- [[Order Service]] — Core Services — authoritative order state and transactional events.
- [[Webhook Gateway]] — Platform & Reliability, with Core Services owning event semantics — external event delivery.

## Customer application

- [[Merchant Console]] — Product Engineering — merchant-facing web application.

Tier-1 expectations are defined in [[Service ownership standard]]. A new production service should not enter this catalog without a named owner, data boundary, operational tier, and recovery path.

The system-level dependency view is in [[Platform architecture]].

action.title: Decision register
action.body:
# Decision register

Accepted decisions constrain both human and agent work. An agent may propose a change to a decision, but it must not silently route around one because a locally convenient implementation differs.

This register points to decisions that materially constrain current engineering work. The decision object holds the reasoning; this page is only the map.

## Accepted

- [[ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction]] — synchronous checkout ends at durable commit; outbound delivery is asynchronous.
- [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]] — queue-backed scheduling with PostgreSQL remaining the recoverable source of event and attempt history.

## Policy decisions

- [[Public API compatibility policy]] — compatibility and deprecation rules for external interfaces.

Create a new decision when the reasoning is likely to matter after the implementation is finished. Do not create an ADR for routine code choices that are obvious from the codebase itself.

When a decision is replaced, preserve the old object, mark its status accordingly, and link the replacement so historical context remains navigable.

action.title: Incident review index
action.body:
# Incident review index

ACME keeps material production incidents and their follow-through together so recurring failure modes are easy to spot.

## 2026

### INC-2026-017 — Checkout latency spike — SEV-2

- Incident record: [[INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike]]
- Review: [[Postmortem: INC-2026-017]]
- Primary system: Checkout API
- Runbook changed: [[Runbook: Checkout latency]]

Key lesson: database connection pools are part of a shared capacity budget. Increasing one application's pool can transfer contention rather than create capacity.

## Review expectations

SEV-1 and SEV-2 incidents require a written review. The review should distinguish trigger, contributing conditions, detection gaps, mitigation quality, and owned follow-up work. The purpose is future operational leverage, not a narrative of who acted incorrectly.

action.title: Human-agent engineering model
action.body:
# Human-agent engineering model

ACME treats software agents as execution environments for engineering work, not as a parallel organization. Humans and agents should discover the same durable context and contribute improvements back to the same knowledge graph.

## Principles

1. **One source of engineering context.** Services, decisions, projects, runbooks, incident learning, and skills live together. We do not maintain a shadow "AI knowledge base."
2. **Delegation is scoped.** Give an agent a concrete objective, relevant context, and the minimum authority required to make progress.
3. **Authorship remains visible.** Agent-assisted output should preserve who requested, reviewed, and accepted the work. A generated patch is not an accepted decision.
4. **Skills are reusable procedures, not hidden prompts.** The canonical procedures are listed in [[Shared engineering skills]] and link to the policies and system knowledge they depend on.
5. **Durable discoveries flow back.** If an agent has to rediscover the same undocumented fact twice, improve the source object or the relevant skill.
6. **Authority is explicit.** Reading, proposing, modifying repositories, deploying, mutating production, and communicating externally are different permissions. See [[Agent access and approval policy]].

## Typical workflow

An engineer starts with an objective and selects a relevant skill. The agent follows the linked service and decision context, performs the permitted work, and returns evidence: changed files, commands run, assumptions, unresolved questions, or incident observations. The human reviewer decides whether the result is accepted.

For repository work start with [[Skill: Implement a repository change]]. For operations start with [[Skill: Triage a production incident]]. For reusable learning use [[Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge]].

action.title: Agent access and approval policy
action.body:
# Agent access and approval policy

Agents are granted capabilities according to task, environment, and data sensitivity. The existence of a command in a runbook or a credential in the surrounding environment is not authorization to use it.

## Default capability levels

### Read and analyze

Allowed for ordinary engineering tasks when the agent is operating in an approved environment. This includes repository search, Kival search, build logs, non-sensitive telemetry, and local tests.

### Prepare changes

Allowed when the task explicitly requests a repository or documentation change. Agents may edit a working tree, run tests, and produce a patch. A human owns merge approval unless a repository has an explicitly documented automated merge policy.

### Production mutation

Requires explicit human approval for the specific action. Examples include deployments, rollbacks, database failover, queue manipulation, feature-flag changes, credential rotation, and modifying customer data.

### External communication

Customer, status-page, regulator, and vendor communication requires a human owner. Agents may draft material but must not publish it autonomously.

## Data boundaries

Follow [[Data classification and handling]]. Do not copy secrets, authentication material, customer payloads, or restricted data into skill bodies or durable agent notes. Agent credentials must be scoped, attributable, revocable, and separate from human credentials; the underlying principles are described in [[Authentication model]].

## Incident rule

During an incident, the human incident commander sets objectives and approves consequential actions. Agents can accelerate diagnosis using Skill: Triage a production incident, but urgency does not broaden their permissions.

action.title: Shared engineering skills
action.body:
# Shared engineering skills

Skills are versioned, reusable procedures for work that ACME expects humans and agents to perform repeatedly. They are intentionally stored beside the systems, policies, decisions, and incidents that give them meaning.

## Software delivery

- [[Skill: Implement a repository change]] — make a bounded code change with evidence.
- [[Skill: Review a public API change]] — check compatibility and rollout implications.
- [[Skill: Prepare a production release]] — assemble a reviewable release packet.

## Operations

- [[Skill: Triage a production incident]] — establish impact, ownership, and first hypotheses.
- [[Skill: Investigate checkout latency]] — diagnose the Checkout API without jumping straight to mitigation.
- [[Skill: Investigate webhook backlog]] — distinguish producer, queue, worker, and downstream failure.
- [[Skill: Assist with database failover]] — prepare and verify failover steps while preserving human approval.

## Learning

- [[Skill: Draft an incident review]] — turn the event record into evidence-backed organizational learning.
- [[Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge]] — promote useful discoveries from transient work into shared memory.

A skill should be short enough to execute, explicit about stopping conditions, and linked rather than duplicated when authoritative context already exists elsewhere.

action.title: Skill: Implement a repository change
action.body:
# Skill: Implement a repository change

**Use when:** an engineer delegates a bounded code change in an existing ACME repository.

## Required context

- The objective and acceptance criteria.
- The owning service from Service catalog.
- Relevant accepted decisions from Decision register.
- Repository-local contribution and test instructions.

## Procedure

1. Inspect the affected code path and its tests before editing.
2. State the smallest coherent change that satisfies the objective.
3. Check whether the change alters public API behavior, persistence, authentication, authorization, or operational failure modes. If yes, follow the relevant policy or decision before implementation.
4. Make the change without unrelated cleanup.
5. Run the narrowest useful tests first, then the repository-required checks.
6. Review the diff as a reviewer would: accidental surface-area changes, error handling, compatibility, logs, metrics, and rollback implications.
7. Return the patch plus commands run, evidence, and unresolved uncertainty.

## Guardrails

Do not reinterpret an accepted architecture decision to make the patch easier. Do not weaken tests or validation merely to make checks pass. Do not merge or deploy unless the task and repository policy explicitly grant that authority.

If durable system knowledge was missing, finish with [[Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge]].

action.title: Skill: Review a public API change
action.body:
# Skill: Review a public API change

**Use when:** a proposed change affects an externally consumed HTTP API, webhook contract, authentication behavior, or documented integration semantics.

## Procedure

1. Identify the exact externally observable change: schema, status code, ordering, default, timing, authentication, idempotency, or error behavior.
2. Read [[Public API compatibility policy]] and any relevant entry in Decision register.
3. Compare the proposed behavior with the currently supported contract and migration state, including API v2 migration when applicable.
4. Classify the change as compatible, conditionally compatible, or breaking. Explain the evidence rather than relying on the label alone.
5. Check rollout and observability: can old and new clients coexist, can adoption be measured, and can the change be reversed?
6. If authentication or cross-tenant access changes, include Authentication model and Security Engineering in review.
7. Produce a concise review with required changes, open questions, and a recommendation.

## Stop and escalate

Do not approve a breaking change by inventing an undocumented exception. If policy and desired product behavior conflict, propose a decision update for human review.

action.title: Skill: Prepare a production release
action.body:
# Skill: Prepare a production release

**Use when:** a change is approaching production and the release owner needs a compact, evidence-backed release packet.

## Procedure

1. Read Production release process and identify the owning team and service tier from Service catalog.
2. Summarize user-visible and operational changes; link the implementation to relevant projects, RFCs, ADRs, or policies.
3. Record CI and test evidence. Flag skipped checks rather than treating absence as success.
4. Identify schema changes, feature flags, configuration changes, background migrations, and dependency-order requirements.
5. State the rollback or forward-fix plan and conditions that would trigger it.
6. Link the dashboard, SLO, and runbook expected during the observation window. For tier-1 changes, confirm on-call ownership from On-call handbook.
7. Return the packet for human release-owner approval.

## Guardrail

This skill prepares a release; it does not authorize deployment. Production mutation follows Agent access and approval policy.

action.title: Skill: Triage a production incident
action.body:
# Skill: Triage a production incident

**Use when:** an alert or report suggests an active production failure and impact is not yet fully understood.

## First pass

1. Establish the symptom, start time, affected tenants or traffic, and whether the failure is ongoing.
2. Identify the likely owning service through Service catalog and open On-call handbook.
3. Collect read-only evidence: SLOs, error rate, latency, saturation, recent deploys, dependency health, and relevant logs or traces.
4. Separate observations from hypotheses. Maintain a short timeline with timestamps and source links.
5. Choose the service-specific runbook or skill if one exists. For checkout use [[Skill: Investigate checkout latency]]; for webhooks use [[Skill: Investigate webhook backlog]].
6. Escalate when impact or ambiguity exceeds the owning team's threshold.

## Guardrails

Do not perform a rollback, failover, queue mutation, feature-flag change, or customer communication without the approval required by Agent access and approval policy. Never turn a plausible hypothesis into incident fact just because it explains several symptoms.

## Output

Return current impact, evidence, hypotheses ranked by support, the next diagnostic step, owner, and any approval needed.

action.title: Skill: Investigate checkout latency
action.body:
# Skill: Investigate checkout latency

**Use when:** Checkout API latency or timeout rate rises above its normal operating envelope.

## Procedure

1. Start with [[Runbook: Checkout latency]] and confirm whether p50, p95, and p99 moved together.
2. Break request time into application work, Order Service calls, database time, and external dependency time.
3. Compare database query latency with connection-pool wait and pool utilization before concluding that PostgreSQL itself is slow.
4. Check deploys, traffic shape, retry amplification, and saturation across instances.
5. Use traces to test the leading hypothesis against both slow and healthy requests.
6. If database availability rather than application contention is suspected, move to Runbook: Database failover; do not initiate failover from this skill.

## Output

Report the earliest divergence, the strongest supporting evidence, disproven hypotheses, and the safest next action. Link any incident record created during the investigation.

action.title: Skill: Investigate webhook backlog
action.body:
# Skill: Investigate webhook backlog

**Use when:** delivery age, queue depth, or retry volume rises for Webhook Gateway.

## Procedure

1. Read Runbook: Webhook backlog and determine whether ingress, queueing, workers, or downstream endpoints are the current bottleneck.
2. Compare publish rate, consume rate, oldest-message age, retry rate, worker saturation, and downstream response classes.
3. Segment by tenant and endpoint before assuming a platform-wide failure.
4. Check recent changes to Project Relay and the accepted design in RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery.
5. Distinguish backlog growth from delivery failure: a growing queue with healthy drain rate may have a different response than repeated poison-message retries.
6. Propose mitigation with expected effect and risk. Queue deletion, replay, or bypass requires human approval.

## Output

Return the constrained stage, evidence, projected recovery direction, and any tenant-specific concentration.

action.title: Skill: Assist with database failover
action.body:
# Skill: Assist with database failover

**Use when:** the incident commander is evaluating or executing the established PostgreSQL failover procedure.

This is an assistance skill around Runbook: Database failover, not an independent authority to fail over production.

## Prepare

1. Confirm the runbook version, affected cluster, incident owner, and explicit approval to proceed.
2. Gather replication health, primary reachability, replica lag, client error rate, and application pool state.
3. Surface any condition in the runbook that makes failover unsafe or ambiguous.
4. Prepare the exact command sequence and expected observations without executing mutating steps.

## During approved execution

Track each human-approved step, timestamp, observed result, and deviation from expected state. Stop on unexpected state rather than improvising a new recovery procedure.

## Verify

Confirm write availability, replica topology, application recovery, error-rate trend, and whether queued or retried work needs follow-up. Capture durable deviations with [[Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge]].

action.title: Skill: Draft an incident review
action.body:
# Skill: Draft an incident review

**Use when:** an incident is stable and the owning team needs to turn the operational record into durable learning.

## Inputs

Use the incident timeline, telemetry, deploy history, relevant service/runbook context, and concrete follow-up evidence. Postmortem: INC-2026-017 is a representative example.

## Procedure

1. State impact and duration in measurable terms.
2. Reconstruct the timeline from evidence. Mark uncertain or reconstructed timestamps.
3. Explain the technical failure chain, including why safeguards did not prevent or rapidly contain it.
4. Separate trigger, contributing conditions, and organizational gaps. Avoid reducing the explanation to the last person who touched the system.
5. Record what worked during detection and response.
6. Propose follow-ups with an owner and verification condition.
7. Check whether a runbook, service page, decision, or reusable skill should change. Closing the ticket without updating shared knowledge is incomplete when the incident exposed a repeatable gap.

## Output

Create or update an entry linked from Incident review index and connect material procedural improvements back into [[Shared engineering skills]].

action.title: Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge
action.body:
# Skill: Capture durable engineering knowledge

**Use when:** a task, review, incident, or agent session uncovers context that will matter beyond the current conversation.

## Decide where it belongs

- Service ownership, dependencies, or operating expectations → Service catalog or the service page.
- Architectural constraint or rationale → Decision register through an ADR/RFC update or new decision.
- Repeatable operational procedure → the relevant runbook or [[Shared engineering skills]].
- Incident-specific evidence and learning → Incident review index.
- Active delivery context → the project page.

## Procedure

1. Capture the smallest durable fact or procedure that would prevent rediscovery.
2. Update the existing canonical object when one exists; avoid near-duplicate notes.
3. Link the new knowledge to the systems and decisions it affects.
4. Preserve uncertainty explicitly. A hypothesis does not become fact by being written down.
5. If a skill changes, keep the procedure executable and explain new stopping conditions or approvals.

## Quality check

A future engineer or agent should be able to discover the knowledge from the affected service or workflow without knowing the original chat, ticket, or prompt that produced it.

# RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery

## Status

Accepted on 2026-08-21 after production shadow-enqueue results matched the database outbox.

## Problem

The current webhook workers use a database polling loop that is reliable but increasingly expensive at peak volume. Large tenants can also create enough retries to delay unrelated tenants.

## Decision

Introduce a durable queue between the transactional outbox and delivery workers. Partition scheduling by tenant, enforce per-tenant concurrency, and keep delivery-attempt history in PostgreSQL for support and auditability.

## Invariants

- Order Service remains the source of event truth.
- A queue message is a delivery instruction, not the only copy of an event.
- Duplicate delivery remains valid behavior.
- Rebuilding queue state from PostgreSQL must be possible.

## Rollout

Shadow-enqueue first, then internal tenants, then 5%, 25%, and 100% of production tenants. The database poller remains the rollback path until two stable weeks at 100%.

## Decision notes

We explicitly rejected queue-only event storage because it would make replay and support depend on queue retention. We also rejected per-tenant queues because operational cardinality would grow with customer count.

Implementation is tracked in [[Project Relay]].

# Project Relay

**Owner:** Charlie  
**Status:** In progress  
**Target:** 100% production webhook traffic by 2026-09-18

Relay implements the accepted [[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]] for Webhook Gateway. Shadow traffic has been stable for six days and internal tenants are now using queue-backed delivery.

## Milestones

- [x] Queue provisioning and metrics
- [x] Shadow enqueue from production outbox
- [x] Internal tenants on queue-backed delivery
- [ ] 5% production canary
- [ ] 25% production
- [ ] 100% production
- [ ] Remove old scheduler after two stable weeks

## Latest findings

Replay from PostgreSQL rebuilt queue state correctly in the recovery test. Tenant partitioning also prevented the synthetic retry-storm tenant from delaying control traffic.

## Guardrails

The old poller remains deployable until final cleanup. Event IDs and attempt history do not change during rollout. A rollback must not require a data migration.

Next decision point: move the 5% canary after 48 hours of stable internal-tenant delivery.

# Checkout API

**Tier:** 1  
**Owner:** Core Services  
**Primary datastore:** PostgreSQL through Order Service

Checkout API is the public synchronous entry point for creating and updating checkout sessions. It validates integration credentials, normalizes requests, applies idempotency rules, and coordinates the order transition with [[Order Service]].

## Reliability target

- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly
- p95 latency target: < 300 ms
- p99 latency target: < 700 ms

Webhook delivery is not part of the synchronous success condition. See ADR 012: Keep webhook delivery off the checkout transaction.

## Capacity guardrails

Following INC-2026-017: Checkout latency spike, bulk-import traffic has a separate concurrency ceiling and connection-acquisition wait is part of the primary dashboard. Application pool limits are treated as database capacity controls, not local tuning knobs.

## Operations

Start with Runbook: Checkout latency. The full incident analysis is in Postmortem: INC-2026-017. Public behavior follows Public API compatibility policy.

# Postmortem: INC-2026-017

## Summary

A bulk-import traffic burst caused Checkout API workers to saturate their PostgreSQL connection pool. Requests queued behind connection acquisition, then retried close enough together to increase pressure. The first mitigation—raising the application pool limit—shifted contention into PostgreSQL and made tail latency worse for several minutes.

## Why safeguards did not catch it

Load tests modeled aggregate request volume but not one tenant producing a burst of expensive writes. Alerts emphasized query duration and CPU; connection-acquisition wait was visible on dashboards but did not page.

## What worked

Per-tenant traffic controls existed and were applied without deployment. Once concurrency was reduced, the system recovered predictably.

## Actions

- [x] Add connection-acquisition wait to the Checkout SLO dashboard.
- [x] Cap bulk-import concurrency independently from interactive checkout.
- [x] Update [[Runbook: Checkout latency]] to warn against unreviewed pool expansion.
- [ ] Add tenant-skew scenarios to the September load test.
- [ ] Review database connection budgets for all tier-1 services.

The review on 2026-08-20 confirmed the first three actions in production. Remaining actions are owned by Platform & Reliability and Core Services.

No individual action caused the incident; the failure came from capacity assumptions and a mitigation path that was insufficiently documented.

# Web performance budget

The Merchant Console should remain usable on ordinary business laptops and imperfect office networks. Performance work is evaluated against user-visible interaction, not bundle size alone.

## Budgets

For the authenticated order list on a warm CDN path:

- initial JavaScript transfer: <= 350 KB compressed;
- Largest Contentful Paint p75: < 2.5 s;
- Interaction to Next Paint p75: < 200 ms;
- route transition to useful content p75: < 800 ms.

## August measurement

The API v2 migration assistant increased the shared shell by 31 KB in its first implementation. It was moved behind the integration route, bringing shared-shell growth down to 6 KB without removing functionality.

## Review triggers

A change that adds more than 25 KB compressed JavaScript to the shared shell needs a short justification. Large optional features should load behind the route or interaction that needs them.

The budget is a constraint for Merchant Console, not a reason to avoid functionality. Update the budget deliberately if product requirements genuinely change the tradeoff.

# Q3 2026 engineering priorities

The quarter is intentionally narrow. Reliability work takes precedence over expanding surface area in the public API.

## 1. Finish Project Relay — on track

[[RFC 024: Asynchronous webhook delivery]] is accepted and internal tenants are live on the new path. Next milestone: 5% production canary. See [[Project Relay]].

## 2. Reduce checkout tail latency — improving

The immediate actions from [[Postmortem: INC-2026-017]] are complete. We still need the September tenant-skew load test before calling the incident class closed.

## 3. Complete API v2 migration — watch

Adoption is 64% of active traffic. Two large generated-client integrations are the critical path. See [[API v2 migration]].

## 4. Tighten operational readiness — active

Tier-1 services are being reviewed against Service ownership standard.

### Explicitly not a priority

A broad service decomposition. We will split systems only when ownership, scaling, or failure isolation requires it; smaller services are not a goal by themselves.

# Skill: Investigate checkout latency

**Use when:** Checkout API latency or timeout rate rises above its normal operating envelope.

This skill was revised after Postmortem: INC-2026-017 because the original investigation over-weighted database query latency and did not make connection-pool contention explicit enough.

## Procedure

1. Start with [[Runbook: Checkout latency]] and confirm whether p50, p95, and p99 moved together.
2. Break request time into application work, Order Service calls, database time, and external dependency time.
3. **Check pool wait before query tuning:** compare `db_pool_wait_seconds`, pool utilization, waiter count, and database query latency. High pool wait with normal query latency points to application-side connection contention, not a slow database.
4. Compare affected instances and deploy generations. A subset of saturated instances can disappear inside aggregate database metrics.
5. Check deploys, traffic shape, retry amplification, request concurrency, and any worker or connection limit changed by the release.
6. Use traces to test the leading hypothesis against both slow and healthy requests.
7. If database availability rather than application contention is suspected, move to Runbook: Database failover; do not initiate failover from this skill.

## Stop conditions

Stop and escalate before mitigation when the proposed action is destructive, affects data consistency, or requires production mutation outside the current approval. Follow Agent access and approval policy.

## Output

Report the earliest divergence, the strongest supporting evidence, disproven hypotheses, and the safest next action. Link any incident record created during the investigation.
I would keep the v1 sunset explicitly conditional on reaching the 90% migration target. We are not close enough to make the date feel inevitable yet.
Agreed. The target is a decision gate, not a promised sunset date. I updated the wording in the migration plan to match that.
Can we make replay semantics more explicit before implementation finishes? I care about what happens when a delivery succeeds remotely but we lose the acknowledgement locally.
Yes. The worker should treat that as an at-least-once case and the public contract needs to say consumers must tolerate duplicate delivery.
I will add the failure matrix to the RFC and link the dashboard fields we use to distinguish retry from first delivery.
The connection-pool alert is still noisy during deploys. Should the warning key off sustained queue time instead of raw utilization?
Yes, utilization alone is not actionable. Keep saturation on the dashboard but page on queue time plus request latency.
Action item 3 needs a named owner and a verification date. Otherwise this is the kind of thing we rediscover next incident.
Assigned to Charlie with the next game day as the verification point.
I want the production read-access section to say scoped and time-bounded explicitly. Read-only is still too broad if an agent can enumerate every tenant.
Makes sense. Platform can issue service-scoped credentials for investigations instead of reusing the general operator role.
Should this skill require the agent to state the test plan before editing? It would make large mechanical patches easier to review.
For non-trivial changes, yes. I would keep tiny documentation-only edits exempt so the skill does not become ceremony.
Please add an explicit handoff point when diagnosis reaches a production mutation. The agent can recommend the runbook step, but the incident commander should own the decision.
Strong +1. That boundary should match the approval policy verbatim so we only have one rule.
Merchant cohort 3 still has two integrations depending on the old pagination behavior. Do we want a compatibility shim or should we hold that cohort?
Hold the cohort for now. A shim would extend behavior we are specifically trying to remove.
Please capture the two blockers in the migration tracker. If the same issue appears in another cohort we can revisit.
Step 6 should say which region is authoritative after promotion. During the last game day we had two people checking different dashboards.
Good catch. I added the control-plane check before application traffic is reopened.
The dependency from Checkout API to the event delivery path is documented, but the escalation owner is not obvious from this page.
I will add Core Services as the application owner and Platform as the infrastructure escalation, rather than a single ambiguous owner field.
This assumes the local development environment is already working before day one. Can we link the bootstrap path directly from the first-day checklist?
Yes. I also want a known-good smoke test there so new engineers can tell setup problems from application problems.
Can we explicitly say that repeated findings should be promoted into durable knowledge instead of accumulating in task transcripts? That is the behavior I want agents to learn.
Yes. I would use three examples: a service fact goes to the service page, a repeatable procedure becomes a skill/runbook, and a trade-off becomes an ADR or RFC.
The backlog section should link the per-destination retry histogram. The aggregate queue depth hid the partner-specific failure last week.
Added to the runbook. I am leaving aggregate depth as the first signal but the next step now breaks it down by destination.
Is the 15 minute canary window still enough for Checkout API? Most of the slow pool failures show up only after traffic has ramped for a while.
For tier-1 services treat 15 minutes as the minimum, not the completion condition. The SLO and saturation signals need to be stable at representative traffic.
The handbook says decisions should be durable, but it does not say when a discussion has crossed the threshold for an ADR. Can we make that trigger less subjective?
Good point. I will use “changes a shared constraint or is expensive to reverse” as the default trigger and keep small local choices in the owning object.
The diagram text still makes the webhook queue look like part of checkout. Can we call out that enqueue is the boundary and delivery is independently recoverable?
Yes. That distinction is also what we use operationally, so I will mirror the wording from the Relay RFC.
Do we still need a named secondary for every incident? For most SEV-3s the second person joins only if escalation is needed.
Not for SEV-3. Keep primary + incident channel, then pull a second engineer when the scope crosses a service boundary or the incident is promoted.
A few skills are getting very service-specific. I think the catalog should distinguish organization-wide skills from service-local skills so agents do not load everything.
Agreed. The catalog should stay small at the top level; service pages can point to the narrower skills that are relevant in that context.
Can we treat error-code removal the same as response-field removal here? Integrators are branching on some of the current codes even though we never documented them well.
Yes for codes we have emitted consistently. Undocumented does not mean unused. I will add error semantics to the compatibility checklist.
For tier-1 services I would add a security contact or reviewed threat model location. “Owning team” is not enough during an auth-related incident.
Makes sense. I prefer linking the reviewed security context rather than naming a person, so the ownership survives team changes.

# Project Atlas: Checkout extraction

action.title: ACME company handbook

# ACME company handbook

ACME builds commerce infrastructure for growing merchants. This workspace is the durable operating memory of the company: decisions, plans, policies, launch context, recruiting practice, engineering knowledge, and reusable skills live here rather than disappearing into chat.

## Operating principles

- Write down decisions that will still matter next quarter.
- Give teams enough context to act without copying every document to everyone.
- Keep sensitive recruiting, people, commercial, and security material deliberately scoped.
- Agents use the same authored knowledge as people; they do not get a parallel hidden handbook.
- Promote repeated work into a skill once the process is stable enough to be reused.

Start with the [[Company directory]], [[ACME operating model]], and [[Q3 2026 company priorities]].

# ACME operating model

ACME runs with small functional teams and explicit cross-functional owners.

## Functional ownership

Engineering owns production systems and technical delivery. Product owns product direction and launch readiness. People owns recruiting and employee operations. Marketing owns brand, demand generation, and advertising. Partnerships owns strategic partner development. Security & Compliance sets security and handling constraints.

## Decisions

A decision belongs with the team that will live with its consequences. Company-level decisions are recorded here when they affect multiple functions or materially change priorities.

## Information boundaries

Company-wide material defaults to readable by everyone. Team working documents are scoped to the relevant group. Candidate notes, performance material, partner negotiation details, and security-sensitive procedures are narrower by design.

See [[Decision and meeting cadence]] for the recurring rhythm and [[Q3 2026 company priorities]] for current company focus.

action.body:
# Q3 2026 company priorities

The company has three priorities for Q3.

## 1. Ship the September platform launch cleanly

The launch should improve merchant activation without turning the quarter into a feature pile. Product owns readiness; Marketing owns the market narrative; Engineering owns reliability; Partnerships owns channel enablement.

## 2. Hire deliberately

Fill the two roles in the current [[2026 hiring plan]] without lowering the bar or allowing interview loops to become bespoke. Hiring quality matters more than speed after the qualified-pipeline threshold is healthy.

## 3. Prove repeatable acquisition

Marketing should establish one paid channel with acceptable payback and one repeatable organic motion. The goal is not maximum lead volume; it is evidence that the company can acquire the right merchants predictably.

## Not a priority

Adding management layers. We will add structure when coordination cost requires it, not because the company crossed an arbitrary headcount.

action.title: Decision and meeting cadence
action.body:
# Decision and meeting cadence

Meetings exist to resolve uncertainty or coordinate action, not to distribute information that could have been authored.

## Weekly

- Monday functional planning inside each team.
- Tuesday leadership operating review: metrics, risks, hiring, launches, and cross-functional decisions.
- Thursday launch/revenue sync only while a launch or active campaign needs it.

## Monthly

Leadership reviews company metrics, cash commitments, hiring capacity, security/compliance risks, and the next six weeks of launches.

## Written first

Material decisions should have a short written brief before the meeting. The decision and rationale are updated after the meeting. Agents may prepare evidence, summarize open questions, and draft the update, but the accountable owner records the final decision.

Use [[Skill: Prepare the weekly operating brief]] for the recurring preparation workflow.

action.title: Company operating metrics
action.body:
# Company operating metrics

This is the leadership view of the business. It is deliberately not company-wide because it combines revenue, hiring capacity, and forward-looking operating assumptions.

## Q3 scorecard

- Net revenue retention: 108% target
- New activated merchants: 140 target
- Qualified pipeline coverage: 3.0× next-quarter new-business target
- Gross margin: >72%
- Tier-1 availability: 99.95% monthly target
- Time-to-fill for approved roles: <55 days median

## Interpretation

A metric is a prompt for investigation, not a target to game. We prefer a smaller set whose causal story can be explained. Functional dashboards can be richer; this page contains the measures that influence company-level trade-offs.

The Tuesday operating review updates commentary when a metric moves enough to change a decision.

action.title: Vendor evaluation and procurement
action.body:
# Vendor evaluation and procurement

ACME keeps procurement lightweight until risk or spend justifies more process.

## Before committing

1. Name an internal owner and the problem being solved.
2. Check whether an existing tool already covers the use case.
3. Record annualized cost and exit difficulty.
4. If the vendor will process customer, employee, or candidate data, involve Security & Compliance before purchase.
5. For material contracts, record renewal date and termination notice window.

## Decision thresholds

Team leads may approve low-cost, reversible tools inside their budget. Leadership reviews material annual commitments, high lock-in, or tools that become operational dependencies.

The objective is not a procurement bureaucracy. It is to avoid discovering a year later that a forgotten tool holds sensitive data or auto-renewed into a material commitment.

action.title: Skill: Prepare the weekly operating brief
action.body:
# Skill: Prepare the weekly operating brief

**Purpose:** Turn current company signals into a short decision-oriented brief for the Tuesday leadership review.

## Inputs

- [[Company operating metrics]]
- [[Q3 2026 company priorities]]
- open launch risks
- approved hiring changes
- material campaign or partner changes

## Procedure

1. Identify movements that could change a decision; ignore routine noise.
2. For each movement, state what changed, likely cause, confidence, and owner.
3. Separate facts from interpretation.
4. Surface decisions needed this week and what happens if they are deferred.
5. Link to the durable source instead of copying long background sections.

## Agent boundary

An agent may gather and synthesize the evidence, but it must not invent missing commercial figures or turn an ambiguous trend into a confident causal claim. Owners validate their section before the brief is treated as authoritative.

action.title: People handbook
action.body:
# People handbook

The People team owns employment operations, recruiting practice, onboarding, and manager guidance. Company-wide policies should be easy to find; personal employment records and candidate assessments are not company-wide knowledge.

## Principles

- Make expectations explicit before using process to enforce them.
- Evaluate candidates against the role, not against whoever interviewed them last.
- Keep candidate and employee data on a need-to-know basis.
- Record decisions and criteria; avoid preserving unnecessary personal detail.
- Treat onboarding as a product that should improve after every cohort.

For current hiring, use [[2026 hiring plan]] and [[Recruiting process]]. For joining ACME, see [[Company onboarding]].

action.title: Recruiting process
action.body:
# Recruiting process

The default loop has five stages. Deviations need a reason recorded before the candidate enters the altered stage.

1. Recruiter screen — motivation, logistics, role basics.
2. Hiring-manager screen — scope, seniority, role-specific evidence.
3. Work sample — realistic task with a clear rubric.
4. Structured panel — two or three focused interviews, not repeated “general fit.”
5. Debrief and decision — evidence first, recommendation second.

## Candidate data

Store only information needed to evaluate or run the process. Do not copy sensitive personal information into general team notes. Candidate assessments belong in the restricted hiring material, not company-wide documents.

For engineering roles, use [[Engineering interview loop]]. For consistent first-pass evaluation, see [[Skill: Screen an inbound candidate]].

action.title: Engineering interview loop
action.body:
# Engineering interview loop

- Hiring-manager screen — Bob

- Systems and failure-mode interview — Charlie
- Values/working-style interview — Bob + one cross-functional partner

action.title: Company onboarding
action.body:
# Company onboarding

Onboarding should get a new hire from “I have access” to “I understand how ACME makes decisions” without requiring a week of meetings.

## Before day one

People prepares accounts, payroll/employment administration, equipment, and a named buddy. The manager prepares a first-week plan and a concrete starter outcome.

## Week one

- Read the company handbook and operating model.
- Meet the direct team and the functions most relevant to the role.
- Complete security and data-handling basics.
- Shadow one real operating ritual rather than attending every recurring meeting.
